title: Rerun visualization
body:
## Summary

Adds `rerun_viz/log_to_rerun.py`, which logs exported recordings to [Rerun](https://rerun.io). The GoPro, ARIS and gantry data can then be scrubbed together in one synchronized 3D scene.

For each recording it shows:

- **3D scene:** the gantry → AR3 → sonar/camera pose chain, built from `calibration/transforms.yaml`, `gantry.csv` and the AR3 pan/tilt/roll in `aris_frame_meta.csv`. This is the same composition as `_create_ar3_df` in `release_1_export.py`. The scene also includes the full AR3 trajectory, the target pose, the GoPro camera frustum, the ARIS field of view as a frustum, and the ARIS returns back-projected into 3D.
- **GoPro:** each frame with its bounding-box label (×3), the ARIS field-of-view outline, and the ARIS returns projected into the image.
- **ARIS polar** images, **time series** of gantry position and AR3 pan/tilt/roll, the target's **textured 3D scan**, and the recording **notes**.
- Two timelines: `aris_frame` and `time` (ARIS timestamp).

The ARIS does not resolve elevation, so the image overlay has two modes (`--overlay-mode`):

- `band` (default): each return is spread over the vertical aperture as a heatmap, weighted by the beam pattern (half strength at the edges).
- `line`: each return is drawn as a point at zero elevation.

## Other changes

- **README:** new "Visualizing the data in Rerun" section covering install, downloading the 1.7 GB Zenodo sample, usage, options and limitations.
- **`requirements.txt`:** adds `rerun-sdk==0.41.0`, `opencv-python-headless==4.10.0.84` and `py7zr==0.22.0`. OpenCV was already used by `view_recording.py` but was not listed. The headless build avoids Qt conflicts with PyQt5.
- **`.gitignore`:** ignores `data_download/` and `.venv*`. It also adds the missing newline at the end of the file.

## Testing

- Logged all five recordings in the Zenodo `sample.7z` and inspected them in the Rerun viewer.
- Pose chain check on the left-to-right sweeps: the target projects into the labelled GoPro boxes and lies inside the ARIS range window.
- Fresh Python 3.12 environment installed from `requirements.txt` (NumPy 2.0.1, OpenCV 4.10, pandas 2.2.2); ran the script in both overlay modes.

## Known limitations

- The 14° vertical aperture is the ARIS Explorer 3000 specification, not a value from the data. It can be changed with `--sonar-elevation`.
- The left/right sign of the ARIS beams follows `prep_2_aris_to_polar.py` and has not been verified independently. The target stays near the centre of the beam, so the effect is small.
- GoPro frames use the `linear` intrinsics without undistortion.
- Camera-to-target alignment is looser in the flyby recordings than in the left-to-right sweeps.

title: Clarification on camera model, mesh coordinate frames, and per-recording sonar–camera extrinsics
body:
Hello,

Thank you for releasing the UXO Dataset 2024 and the associated processing tools. I am currently using the dataset for research on geometry-guided alignment between ARIS sonar data and GoPro images, followed by underwater object detection and instance segmentation.

My intended workflow is:

1. Recover the target, sonar, and camera coordinate transforms.
2. Project points from the released UXO 3D models into both the GoPro image and the ARIS polar image.
3. Build a target-aware geometrically aligned sonar map in the camera coordinate system.
4. Use the aligned RGB–sonar data for object detection or instance segmentation.

I have completed an initial audit of the released data and code:

- 94 recording directories were found locally.
- 74,437 ARIS frames were indexed.
- 48,462 matched GoPro frames were indexed.
- The calibration files distributed with the data match the files in the GitHub repository.
- All 11 static transforms parsed from `transforms.yaml` are valid rigid-body transforms.
- The official recording viewer runs successfully.
- Raw ARIS frames can be converted into reference polar images using the released processing code.
- The released 3D models can be loaded successfully.

However, I cannot yet complete a verifiable target-level sonar–camera projection because several coordinate and imaging conventions are unclear. I would greatly appreciate clarification on the following points.

## 1. GoPro image mode used for the exported frames

The calibration directory contains camera parameters for multiple modes, such as:

- `linear`
- `narrow`
- `wide`
- `superview`

Which mode corresponds to the exported GoPro JPG images in the recording folders?

Was the same GoPro mode used for all recordings, or can it vary between recordings?

If it varies, is the mode stored in any recording-specific metadata file?

## 2. Camera projection and distortion model

What projection model should be used with the four distortion coefficients in the camera parameter files?

Specifically, are these coefficients intended for:

- OpenCV standard Brown–Conrady distortion,
- `cv2.fisheye` / equidistant fisheye projection,
- a GoPro-specific projection model,
- or another model?

Could you also confirm:

- the coefficient order;
- the image resolution for which the intrinsics were calibrated;
- whether the released JPG frames are raw, digitally cropped, stabilized, or already undistorted;
- whether the camera matrix needs to be scaled before it is applied to the released images?

A small example using `cv2.projectPoints`, `cv2.fisheye.projectPoints`, or the intended alternative would be extremely helpful.

## 3. Coordinate frame of the released 3D models

For each released OBJ model, could you clarify:

- the unit of the vertex coordinates, for example metres or millimetres;
- the location of the model origin;
- the directions of the model X, Y, and Z axes;
- whether the model is centred at its geometric centre, centre of mass, or another reference point;
- whether the object pose is already baked into the OBJ vertices.

Most importantly, is the OBJ model frame identical to the corresponding frame in `transforms.yaml`, such as:

- `target/100lbs`
- `target/incendiary`
- `target/mortar_shell`

In other words, can the model vertices be treated directly as points in the corresponding `target/<type>` frame?

If not, could you provide the missing transform:

`T_target_from_model`

for each target type?

## 4. Direction convention of the target transforms

Could you confirm the precise direction of the target transforms stored in `transforms.yaml`?

For example, does the target entry represent:

`T_world_from_target`

meaning that it transforms a point expressed in the target frame into the world/setup frame?

A short mathematical definition of the transform convention would help avoid an accidental inversion.

## 5. Three-dimensional sonar coordinate convention

Could you provide the exact 3D axis convention of the frame used for the ARIS sonar?

In particular:

- Which axis points forward along the acoustic axis?
- Which axis points to the sonar's right or left?
- Which axis points upward or downward?
- What is the origin of the sonar frame?
- What sign convention is used for bearing?
- How are the 3D axes related to the beam ordering used in `prep_2_aris_to_polar.py`?
- Is a positive bearing located on the left or the right side of the displayed polar image?
- Does the released polar image contain any horizontal or vertical flip relative to the physical sonar frame?

For a point expressed as:

`p_sonar = [x, y, z]`

it would be helpful to know the exact formulas used to obtain:

- slant range;
- horizontal bearing;
- elevation angle;
- ARIS range-bin index;
- ARIS beam index.

I understand that a 2D forward-looking sonar measurement does not uniquely determine elevation. My intended alignment is therefore target-aware: the known 3D target surface supplies the missing elevation information.

## 6. Per-recording GoPro–ARIS extrinsic changes

The paper notes that the transform between the GoPro and ARIS was not perfectly fixed and could move slightly after GoPro battery changes.

Does the released dataset contain any per-recording correction for this movement?

More specifically:

- Is the camera–sonar transform in `transforms.yaml` only a nominal transform?
- Are recording-specific camera poses or correction transforms stored elsewhere?
- Were the GoPro and ARIS physically moved together, or could their relative rotation and translation change independently?
- Were any recordings captured after a battery change without repeating the camera–sonar calibration?
- Is there a mapping between recording IDs and the applicable camera extrinsic calibration?

This point is particularly important for assessing whether target-level geometric projection can be treated as ground truth or only as an approximate initial alignment.

## 7. Validation example

Could you provide one reference example for validating an implementation?

Any one of the following would be sufficient:

- one recording ID and frame ID with the expected projected target centre in the GoPro image;
- one 3D target point together with its expected camera pixel and ARIS range/bearing coordinates;
- one example target mask obtained from the 3D model projection;
- a script used internally to project a released target model into a GoPro frame;
- a complete transform chain for one frame.

This would make it possible to verify the camera model, transform directions, model scale, and sonar axis convention independently.

## 8. Number of recordings

The paper reports 95 recordings, while I find 94 recording directories in the current released `data_export_recordings` archive.

Is one recording intentionally excluded from the public archive, or is one recording stored in a different location or under a different directory structure?

The total number of ARIS frames still matches the reported value of 74,437.

## Current safety boundary in my implementation

At present, my implementation intentionally stops before producing projected masks or aligned sonar maps because the following items cannot yet be verified from the public files alone:

- the exact camera distortion model;
- the model-to-target transform;
- the 3D sonar axis convention;
- possible per-recording camera–sonar extrinsic corrections.

I have therefore not treated any manually adjusted projection as ground-truth alignment.

Once these conventions are clarified, I plan to release a reproducible preprocessing pipeline that produces:

- target-aware sonar-to-camera correspondences;
- aligned target sonar maps;
- valid masks;
- geometry-confidence maps;
- projection-error metrics;
- data suitable for geometry-guided RGB–sonar detection and instance segmentation.

Thank you very much for your time and for making this dataset publicly available.

[projection_blockers.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29992752/projection_blockers.json)

[stage1_final_report.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29992758/stage1_final_report.md)

title: Questions about the transformation between optics and sonar
body: I appreciate your contribution to this field. In 2007, Prof Shariar  Negahdaripour introduce the concept of epipolar geometry of optic-acoustic stereo imaging. I am wondering if you provide any source code to transform from optics to sonar or reverse.
